04-01.script:
The first of April is a day for tricks and laughter. In France, children tape paper fish to the backs of unsuspecting friends and shout poisson d'avril, April fish!

The most famous April Fool of all came in 1957, when the BBC showed a serious news report about Swiss farmers harvesting spaghetti from trees. Hundreds of viewers phoned to ask how they could grow their own.

But real history happened today too. In 1976, in a garage in California, Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne founded a little company called Apple.

In 1960, America launched TIROS-1, the first weather satellite, and for the first time people saw clouds swirling over the Earth from above.

In 1936, Odisha became a separate province of India, and Odias celebrate Utkal Divas today.

And in 2004, Google launched a free email service with a remarkable amount of storage. Because of the date, many thought Gmail was a joke. It was not.

04-02.script:
On the second of April in 1805, in the Danish town of Odense, a shoemaker's son named Hans Christian Andersen was born. He would write of an ugly duckling who became a swan, a little mermaid, and an emperor with no clothes. On his birthday, the world celebrates children's books.

In 1513, Juan Ponce de León stepped ashore on the coast he had named Florida.

In 1800, in Vienna, a young composer named Ludwig van Beethoven presented his First Symphony.

In 1845, two French physicists, Fizeau and Foucault, took the first detailed photograph of the Sun.

In 1917, President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress to declare war on Germany, saying that the world must be made safe for democracy.

And in 1982, Argentine forces landed on the Falkland Islands, beginning a short, bitter war with Britain over a few windswept islands in the South Atlantic.

Today is also World Autism Awareness Day, a day for understanding and acceptance.

04-03.script:
On the third of April in 1860, a young rider galloped out of St. Joseph, Missouri, a leather pouch of letters slung across his saddle. Another set out from Sacramento. The Pony Express had begun, racing the mail nearly three thousand kilometres across the West in about ten days.

In 1882, the outlaw Jesse James was shot dead in his own home, by a member of his gang.

In 1933, two biplanes climbed over the Himalayas and flew above the summit of Mount Everest for the first time, their crews gasping for oxygen as they photographed the roof of the world.

In 1968, on a stormy night in Memphis, Martin Luther King Jr. told a crowd that he had been to the mountaintop, and seen the promised land. I may not get there with you, he said. The next day, he was killed.

And in 1973, on a New York street, an engineer named Martin Cooper lifted a heavy brick of a phone and made the first handheld mobile phone call. He rang a rival company to tell them.

04-04.script:
On the fourth of April in 1581, Queen Elizabeth the First stepped aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford and knighted its captain, Francis Drake, the first Englishman to sail around the world.

In 1949, twelve nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, promising that an attack on one would be an attack on all. NATO was born.

In 1968, on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed. He was thirty-nine. Riots and grief swept across America, but his dream did not die with him.

In 1975, two young friends, Bill Gates and Paul Allen, founded a small company in Albuquerque to write software for a new home computer. They called it Micro-Soft.

And in 1983, the Space Shuttle Challenger roared into the sky on its first flight. On that mission, astronauts made the first spacewalk of the shuttle era.

Today, Senegal celebrates its independence, won in 1960.

04-05.script:
On the fifth of April in 1722, a Dutch explorer named Jacob Roggeveen sighted a small, lonely island in the Pacific. It was Easter Sunday, so he named it Easter Island. Standing on its hillsides were nearly a thousand giant stone heads, gazing inland.

In 1621, the Mayflower sailed home to England, leaving the Pilgrims to face their first spring in the New World.

In 1919, the SS Loyalty, owned by an Indian company, set sail from Bombay to London. It was a bold step for Indian shipping under British rule, and India celebrates National Maritime Day in its memory.

Around this time of year in China, families celebrate Qingming, the festival of clear brightness. They visit their ancestors' graves, sweep them clean, and leave flowers and food.

In 1955, Winston Churchill, aged eighty, resigned as Prime Minister of Britain.

And in 1958, engineers in Canada set off one of the largest non-nuclear explosions in history to blow the top off Ripple Rock, a hidden underwater peak that had wrecked more than a hundred ships.

04-06.script:
On the sixth of April in 1896, in a gleaming marble stadium in Athens, King George of Greece declared the first modern Olympic Games open. Athletes from fourteen nations had come together, reviving a tradition more than fifteen hundred years old.

In 1320, Scottish nobles sent a letter to the Pope declaring their freedom. As long as a hundred of us remain alive, they wrote, we will never submit to English rule. Scots around the world celebrate Tartan Day in its memory.

In 1909, the American explorer Robert Peary claimed to have reached the North Pole with Matthew Henson and four Inuit companions.

In 1930, at the end of his long Salt March, Gandhi bent down on the beach at Dandi and picked up a handful of salt, defying the British law. Millions followed his example.

And in 1974, a Swedish band in glittering costumes won the Eurovision Song Contest with a song called Waterloo. ABBA's story was only beginning.

04-07.script:
On the seventh of April in 1795, France adopted a new and simple system of measurement. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator. Today almost the whole world measures in metres.

In 1906, Mount Vesuvius erupted violently above Naples, and the city that was to host the Olympic Games that year had to give them up. They went to London instead.

In 1927, the American Secretary of Commerce, Herbert Hoover, appeared on a screen in New York while speaking in Washington, in one of the first public demonstrations of long-distance television.

In 1948, the World Health Organization was founded, to bring health to every corner of the world. The whole world now marks World Health Day.

And in 1969, a graduate student named Steve Crocker wrote the first Request for Comments, a humble note about how computers might talk to one another. He wrote it late at night, in a bathroom, so as not to wake his housemates. Those notes still shape the internet.

04-08.script:
On the eighth of April in Japan, temples celebrate the birthday of the Buddha with flowers, and visitors pour sweet tea over small statues of the baby Buddha.

In 1820, a farmer digging on the Greek island of Milos found a beautiful marble statue of a woman, her arms already lost. The Venus de Milo now stands in the Louvre.

In 1857, Mangal Pandey, the soldier who had defied his officers at Barrackpore, was hanged. And on this day in 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi, shouting long live the revolution, and waited calmly to be arrested.

In 1911, a Dutch physicist named Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury close to absolute zero, and found that it suddenly lost all resistance to electricity. He had discovered superconductivity.

And in 1974, in Atlanta, Hank Aaron hit his seven hundred and fifteenth home run, breaking Babe Ruth's long-standing record.

04-09.script:
On the ninth of April in 1865, in the parlour of a farmhouse at Appomattox Court House in Virginia, General Robert E. Lee surrendered his army to General Ulysses Grant. Grant let the hungry Confederate soldiers keep their horses for the spring ploughing. The Civil War was ending.

In 1860, a Frenchman named Édouard-Léon Scott recorded someone singing a folk song, Au clair de la lune, on a machine that traced sound waves onto soot-covered paper. In 2008, scientists played it back. It is the oldest recording of a human voice ever found.

In 1939, refused permission to sing in a concert hall in Washington because she was Black, Marian Anderson sang instead on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, before a crowd of seventy-five thousand.

And in 1959, NASA introduced America to seven test pilots chosen to fly into space: the Mercury Seven.

Canada remembers Vimy Ridge today, where in 1917 its four divisions fought together for the first time, and won.

04-10.script:
On the tenth of April in 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa exploded in the largest eruption in recorded history. Ash filled the sky around the world, and the next year Europe and America had no summer. Crops failed, and in a gloomy Swiss villa, a young writer named Mary Shelley began a story called Frankenstein.

In 1912, the RMS Titanic set sail from Southampton on her maiden voyage, the largest ship in the world, called unsinkable.

In 1925, F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby, a story of green lights, lavish parties and dreams that slip away.

In 1970, Paul McCartney announced that he had left the Beatles. The band that had changed music was no more.

And in 2019, astronomers revealed the first picture ever taken of a black hole: a glowing ring of fire around a dark shadow, at the heart of a galaxy fifty-five million light-years away.

04-11.script:
On the eleventh of April in 1814, at the palace of Fontainebleau, Napoleon Bonaparte signed away his throne. He would be sent to rule the tiny island of Elba. He would not stay there long.

In 1869, in Porbandar, a girl named Kasturba was born. She would marry Mohandas Gandhi at thirteen, and walk beside him through every struggle, prison and march. India celebrates National Safe Motherhood Day on her birthday.

In 1945, American soldiers reached the concentration camp of Buchenwald and found more than twenty thousand prisoners still alive, starving but free.

In 1951, President Truman dismissed General Douglas MacArthur, the hero of the Pacific, for publicly disagreeing with him over the Korean War.

And in 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off towards the Moon. Its crew, Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise, did not yet know that the next few days would become one of the greatest rescue stories ever told.

names: International Day of Human Space Flight
04-12.script:
On the twelfth of April in 1961, at Baikonur in Kazakhstan, a young Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin climbed into a small round capsule called Vostok. As the rocket roared to life, he called out: Poyekhali! Let's go! For one hundred and eight minutes he circled the Earth, the first human ever to see our planet from space. He said it was blue, and beautiful.

Exactly twenty years later, in 1981, America launched a new kind of spacecraft, one that could fly back and land like a plane: the Space Shuttle Columbia.

In 1861, Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, and the American Civil War began.

In 1945, in Warm Springs, Georgia, President Franklin Roosevelt died, just weeks before the victory he had worked for.

And in 1955, scientists announced that Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was safe and effective. Church bells rang across America.

All over the world tonight, people gather for Yuri's Night, to celebrate the dream of spaceflight.

04-13.script:
On the thirteenth of April, as the wheat ripens in Punjab, people celebrate Baisakhi with dancing and drums. It was on Baisakhi in 1699 that Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, the community of the Sikhs, at Anandpur Sahib.

But in 1919, on Baisakhi, thousands had gathered peacefully in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. General Dyer blocked the only exit and ordered his soldiers to fire. Hundreds were killed. The massacre turned millions of Indians against British rule for good.

Far away, in 1742, in Dublin, Handel's Messiah was performed for the first time, as a charity concert for prisoners and the sick.

In 1970, two days into their journey, an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13. Houston, we've had a problem, said Jack Swigert. The Moon landing was off. Now the only goal was to bring the crew home alive.

And in Thailand, the new year of Songkran begins, and the streets fill with laughter as people splash each other with water.

04-14.script:
On the fourteenth of April in 1891, in a military town in central India, Bhimrao Ambedkar was born into a family that society called untouchable. As a boy he was made to sit apart from his classmates. He grew up to earn doctorates from New York and London, to fight for the dignity of the oppressed, and to lead the drafting of India's Constitution. India celebrates his birthday today, along with the new year in Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

On this night in 1865, at Ford's Theatre in Washington, President Abraham Lincoln was shot as he watched a comedy. He died the next morning.

And on the night of the fourteenth of April in 1912, the Titanic, steaming fast through calm, freezing water, struck an iceberg. Within three hours, the unsinkable ship would be gone.

In 1935, a giant wall of dust rolled across the American plains, turning day into night. It was called Black Sunday.

And in 2003, scientists announced that the Human Genome Project was complete: the whole instruction book of human life, read letter by letter.

04-15.script:
On the fifteenth of April in 1452, in the Tuscan village of Vinci, Leonardo was born. He would paint the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, and fill notebooks with flying machines, flowing water and the workings of the human heart. The world celebrates art on his birthday.

In 1755, Samuel Johnson published his great Dictionary of the English Language, after nine years of work. He defined a lexicographer, with a wink, as a harmless drudge.

In the cold small hours of this day in 1912, the Titanic slipped beneath the North Atlantic. More than fifteen hundred people were lost. The ship Carpathia raced through the ice to rescue the survivors from the lifeboats.

In 1947, Jackie Robinson stepped onto the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers, the first Black player in modern major league baseball. Every player in the major leagues now wears his number, 42, on this day.

And in 2019, flames tore through the roof of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, as the whole world watched and held its breath.

04-16.script:
On the sixteenth of April in 1746, on a cold, wet moor near Inverness called Culloden, the Jacobite army of Bonnie Prince Charlie was crushed in less than an hour. It was the last pitched battle fought on British soil, and the old Highland way of life would soon be swept away.

In 1853, three steam engines named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan pulled India's first passenger train out of Bori Bunder in Bombay, on a thirty-four kilometre journey to Thane, to a salute of twenty-one guns.

In 1889, in London, Charlie Chaplin was born. Twenty-five years later, in a bowler hat and baggy trousers, his little tramp would make the whole world laugh.

In 1912, Harriet Quimby flew across the English Channel, the first woman ever to do so.

In 1917, Lenin arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd, returning from exile to lead a revolution.

And in 1963, from a cell in Birmingham jail, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote a letter: injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.

04-17.script:
On the seventeenth of April in 1492, in the Spanish camp at Santa Fe, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella signed a contract with a Genoese sailor named Christopher Columbus, agreeing to back his voyage west across the ocean.

In 1521, Martin Luther stood before the Holy Roman Emperor at the Diet of Worms and was told to take back his writings. He asked for a night to think. The next day he refused, saying, it is said, here I stand, I can do no other.

In 1790, Benjamin Franklin died in Philadelphia, aged eighty-four. Twenty thousand people came to his funeral.

In 1964, Ford unveiled a sporty new car at the New York World's Fair: the Mustang. And on that same day, a housewife from Ohio named Jerrie Mock landed in Columbus, the first woman to fly solo around the world.

And in 1970, after four tense days, the crippled Apollo 13 splashed down safely in the Pacific. The whole world had been holding its breath, and now it cheered.

04-18.script:
On the night of the eighteenth of April in 1775, a silversmith named Paul Revere galloped through the Massachusetts countryside, warning that British troops were on the march. By dawn, the militia were waiting.

In the early morning of this day in 1906, the ground beneath San Francisco shook for less than a minute. Then came the fires, burning for three days. Much of the city was destroyed, and was then rebuilt.

In 1930, the BBC's evening news announcer told listeners: there is no news. And then played piano music for the rest of the bulletin.

In 1942, sixteen American bombers took off from an aircraft carrier in the Pacific, led by Jimmy Doolittle, to strike Tokyo. It was a daring raid that lifted the spirits of a nation.

In 1949, Ireland left the Commonwealth and became a republic.

And in 1955, in Princeton, Albert Einstein died. On the table beside his bed lay his notes on a theory he was still working on.

Today is World Heritage Day, a day to celebrate the monuments and places that belong to us all.

facts.text: World Heritage Day was created in 1982 to celebrate the world's monuments and sites.
On 18 April 1930, the BBC's evening bulletin simply said "There is no news", then played piano music.

04-19.script:
In the grey dawn of the nineteenth of April in 1775, on the village green at Lexington, Massachusetts, a line of farmers faced a column of British soldiers. A shot rang out. No one knows who fired it. The American Revolution had begun, with what a poet would later call the shot heard round the world.

In 1882, Charles Darwin died at his home in Kent. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, near Isaac Newton.

In 1943, the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto rose up against the Nazis, holding out for nearly a month with a handful of weapons.

That same day, in Switzerland, the chemist Albert Hofmann swallowed a tiny dose of a substance he had made, and rode his bicycle home through a world that had turned strange.

In 1965, an engineer named Gordon Moore predicted that the number of parts on a computer chip would double regularly for years to come. Moore's Law held true for half a century.

And in 1975, India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched into space.

events.text: The Battles of Lexington and Concord begin the American Revolutionary War.
The Treaty of London guarantees Belgium's neutrality.
Benjamin Disraeli dies.
Charles Darwin dies.
The first Boston Marathon is run.
The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising begins.
Albert Hofmann takes the first intentional dose of LSD.
Grace Kelly marries Prince Rainier of Monaco.
Gordon Moore publishes the article behind Moore's Law.
The Soviet Union launches Salyut 1, the first space station.
India's first satellite, Aryabhata, is launched.
The Simpsons first appear, in short cartoons on The Tracey Ullman Show.
A bomb destroys a federal building in Oklahoma City.

births.text: Anju Bobby George, Indian long jumper

facts.text: Primrose Day remembers Benjamin Disraeli, whose favourite flower was said to be the primrose.
India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was named after the ancient Indian mathematician.

04-20.script:
On the twentieth of April in 1534, the French explorer Jacques Cartier sailed from Saint-Malo, bound across the Atlantic. His voyages would lead him up a great river he named the St Lawrence, and give a land its name: Canada, from a word for village.

In 1862, in Paris, Louis Pasteur and Claude Bernard completed their first test of a simple idea: heating wine and milk just enough to kill the germs inside. We call it pasteurisation.

In 1902, Marie and Pierre Curie succeeded in isolating a tiny amount of radium salt, after processing tonnes of ore in a leaky shed.

In 1912, two great ballparks opened: Fenway Park in Boston on this day, and Tiger Stadium in Detroit.

In 1972, Apollo 16 landed in the highlands of the Moon. Its astronauts drove their rover across the dusty hills and collected the oldest rocks yet found.

And in 1980, Fidel Castro announced that Cubans who wished to leave could go. Over the next months, more than a hundred thousand sailed to Florida in the Mariel boatlift.

events.text: Jacques Cartier sets sail on his first voyage to Canada.
Oliver Cromwell dissolves the Rump Parliament.
Louis Pasteur and Claude Bernard complete their first test of pasteurisation.
The Civil Rights Act of 1871 is signed against the Ku Klux Klan.
Marie and Pierre Curie isolate radium salts.
Fenway Park opens in Boston.
The Chicago Cubs play their first game at Wrigley Field.
RCA demonstrates its electron microscope.
The Bay of Pigs invasion fails.
Apollo 16 lands on the Moon.
The Mariel boatlift from Cuba begins.
The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert is held at Wembley.
The Deepwater Horizon oil rig explodes in the Gulf of Mexico.

births.text: Napoleon III, Emperor of the French

facts.text: UN Chinese Language Day honours Cangjie, the legendary inventor of Chinese characters.
Canada's name probably comes from "kanata", an Iroquoian word for village.

04-21.script:
The twenty-first of April is the birthday of Rome. Legend says that on this day in 753 BC, Romulus ploughed a furrow around the Palatine Hill and founded the city that would rule the Mediterranean world.

In 1526, at Panipat, north of Delhi, Babur's small army, armed with cannon, defeated the Sultan of Delhi and founded the Mughal Empire.

In 1836, at San Jacinto, Sam Houston's Texans surprised the Mexican army during its afternoon rest. The battle lasted eighteen minutes, and Texas won its independence.

In 1910, Mark Twain died. He had been born when Halley's Comet blazed in the sky, and said he expected to go out with it. The comet had just returned.

In 1926, in London, a baby princess was born, Elizabeth, who would reign for seventy years.

And in 1960, Brazil inaugurated a brand-new capital, built from nothing in four years in the middle of the country: Brasília, shaped like an aeroplane, or a bird in flight.

events.text: Babur defeats the Sultan of Delhi at the First Battle of Panipat.
Brazilian independence hero Tiradentes is executed.
Texans win the Battle of San Jacinto.
The Spanish–American War begins.
Mark Twain dies as Halley's Comet returns, just as he predicted.
The Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, is shot down and killed.
The "surgeon's photograph" of the Loch Ness Monster is published; it is later revealed as a hoax.
Brasília becomes the capital of Brazil.
The Seattle World's Fair opens with its Space Needle.
Haile Selassie visits Jamaica, a day Rastafarians celebrate as Grounation Day.
Colonels seize power in Greece.
The musical Annie opens on Broadway.
The musician Prince dies.

births.text: Friedrich Fröbel, German founder of kindergarten
Elizabeth II, Queen of the United Kingdom

facts.text: Rome celebrates its birthday on 21 April, when Romulus is said to have founded the city in 753 BC.
India's Civil Services Day marks Sardar Patel's 1947 speech calling civil servants "the steel frame of India".

04-22.script:
On the twenty-second of April in 1970, twenty million Americans poured into parks and streets for the first Earth Day, to call for clean air, clean water and care for the planet. Within months, America had new laws to protect its environment. Today, Earth Day is marked in nearly every country on Earth.

In 1500, the Portuguese explorer Pedro Álvares Cabral, sailing for India, saw a mountain rising from the sea, and landed on the coast of Brazil.

In 1889, at the sound of a gunshot at noon, fifty thousand settlers raced on horseback and in wagons into Oklahoma, to claim land. By nightfall, whole towns had sprung up.

In 1915, at Ypres in Belgium, German troops released clouds of chlorine gas, the first large-scale use of poison gas in war.

And in 1993, a free program called Mosaic was released, the first web browser to show pictures alongside words. It opened the World Wide Web to everyone.

events.text: Pedro Álvares Cabral lands in Brazil.
The U.S. Congress approves "In God We Trust" on coins.
The Oklahoma Land Rush begins.
Poison gas is used on a large scale for the first time, at Ypres.
The Army–McCarthy hearings begin on television.
The New York World's Fair opens.
The first Earth Day is celebrated.
Optical fibre first carries live telephone traffic.
The Mosaic web browser is released.
Former U.S. President Richard Nixon dies.
The Paris Agreement on climate change is signed by 175 parties.

facts.text: The first Earth Day in 1970 brought about 20 million Americans onto the streets.
Earth Day was the idea of U.S. Senator Gaylord Nelson.

04-23.script:
The twenty-third of April belongs to books. In 1616, around this date, two of the greatest writers who ever lived died: William Shakespeare in Stratford, and Miguel de Cervantes in Madrid. Shakespeare is also said to have been born on this day, in 1564. The world now celebrates World Book Day, and in Catalonia, people give one another a book and a rose.

It is St George's Day, too, for the soldier saint who slew the dragon, patron of England and many other lands.

In 1014, at Clontarf near Dublin, the Irish High King Brian Boru defeated the Vikings and their allies, though he was killed in the hour of victory.

In 1920, Turkey's Grand National Assembly met for the first time in Ankara, and Turkish children celebrate today as their own.

And in 2005, a young man stood in front of the elephants at San Diego Zoo and said their trunks were really, really long. Me at the Zoo, nineteen seconds long, was the first video ever uploaded to YouTube.

events.text: Brian Boru defeats the Vikings at the Battle of Clontarf.
William Shakespeare dies.
Charles II is crowned King of England.
Edison's Vitascope gives one of the first public film shows in the United States.
Turkey's Grand National Assembly meets for the first time.
The Soviet Union launches Soyuz 1.

Eritreans vote for independence from Ethiopia.
The first YouTube video, "Me at the zoo", is uploaded.

births.text: J. M. W. Turner, English painter
James Buchanan, 15th President of the United States

facts.text: World Book Day honours Shakespeare, Cervantes and Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, who all died around 23 April 1616.
The first YouTube video, "Me at the zoo", is just 19 seconds long.

04-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of April in 1800, the United States Congress set aside five thousand dollars to buy books for its own use. The Library of Congress would grow into the largest library in the world.

In 1915, Ottoman authorities arrested hundreds of Armenian leaders in Constantinople. It was the beginning of the Armenian genocide, in which around a million people died. Armenians remember them on this day.

In 1916, on Easter Monday, Irish rebels seized the General Post Office in Dublin and proclaimed an Irish Republic. The Easter Rising lasted six days, but its leaders' executions turned Ireland towards independence.

In 1970, China launched its first satellite, which circled the Earth playing the song The East Is Red.

And in 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. At first its pictures were blurred by a tiny flaw in its mirror. Astronauts fixed it, and Hubble went on to show us galaxies at the edge of time.

events.text: The Boston News-Letter, the first regular newspaper in the American colonies, is published.
The Library of Congress is founded.
The Woolworth Building, then the world's tallest, opens in New York.
Armenian leaders are arrested in Constantinople, beginning the Armenian genocide.
The Easter Rising begins in Dublin.
Winston Churchill is knighted by Queen Elizabeth II.
Cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov dies when Soyuz 1's parachute fails.
China launches its first satellite, Dong Fang Hong 1.
A U.S. mission to rescue hostages in Iran fails.
The Hubble Space Telescope is launched.
India's 73rd Amendment, giving power to village councils, comes into force.
The Rana Plaza factory building collapses in Bangladesh.

facts.text: China's first satellite played the song "The East Is Red" from orbit.
Hubble's first images were blurry because its main mirror was very slightly misshapen; astronauts fixed it in 1993.

04-25.script:
At dawn on the twenty-fifth of April in 1915, soldiers from Australia and New Zealand rowed ashore on the beaches of Gallipoli, in Turkey. They faced steep cliffs and fierce fire, and thousands never came home. Every year at dawn on ANZAC Day, people gather in silence to remember them.

In 1719, a novel appeared in London about a sailor shipwrecked alone on an island for twenty-eight years. Robinson Crusoe became one of the most famous books ever written.

In 1792, in Strasbourg, an army officer named Rouget de Lisle wrote a war song overnight. Soldiers from Marseille later sang it as they marched into Paris, and La Marseillaise became the anthem of France.

In 1953, a short paper by Watson and Crick appeared in the journal Nature, describing the double helix of DNA.

And in 1974, in Lisbon, soldiers overthrew Portugal's dictatorship almost without a shot. People put red carnations into the barrels of their rifles, and it became known as the Carnation Revolution.

events.text: Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe is published.
Rouget de Lisle composes La Marseillaise.
Construction of the Suez Canal begins.
New York becomes the first U.S. state to require licence plates on cars.
Australian and New Zealand troops land at Gallipoli.
Italy is liberated as the Nazis are driven out.
Delegates meet in San Francisco to found the United Nations.
Watson and Crick publish the structure of DNA.
Bell Labs announces the first practical silicon solar cell.
The Carnation Revolution restores democracy in Portugal.
Israel completes its return of the Sinai to Egypt.
A devastating earthquake strikes Nepal.

facts.text: Portugal's Carnation Revolution is named after the carnations people put in soldiers' rifles.
La Marseillaise is named after volunteers from Marseille who sang it marching into Paris.

04-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of April in 1564, in Stratford-upon-Avon, a baby was baptised as William, son of John Shakespeare. He would write thirty-seven plays and give the English language thousands of words and phrases we still use.

In 1803, a shower of thousands of stones fell from the sky over the French town of L'Aigle. A young scientist sent to investigate proved, at last, that rocks really do fall from space.

In 1937, German and Italian planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica on market day. Pablo Picasso poured his horror into an enormous painting that became a cry against all war.

In 1956, a converted tanker called the Ideal X sailed from New Jersey carrying fifty-eight metal boxes. The shipping container had been born, and world trade would never be the same.

And in 1986, at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine, a reactor exploded during a safety test. Clouds of radiation drifted across Europe, and the nearby town of Pripyat was abandoned. It remains empty today.

events.text: William Shakespeare is baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon.
A shower of meteorites falls at L'Aigle, France, proving that rocks fall from space.
John Wilkes Booth, Lincoln's assassin, is killed.
The Duke of York marries Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, the future Queen Mother.
The Gestapo is founded in Nazi Germany.
German and Italian planes bomb Guernica.

NASA's Ranger 4 crashes into the Moon.
Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite to form Tanzania.
The convention creating the World Intellectual Property Organization comes into force.
A reactor explodes at the Chernobyl nuclear plant.

births.text: John James Audubon, American bird artist

facts.text: Picasso's Guernica is almost 8 metres wide.

04-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of April in 1994, millions of South Africans stood in queues that stretched for kilometres, many of them voting for the very first time. Among them was Nelson Mandela, seventy-five years old, casting his first vote ever. Apartheid was over. South Africa celebrates Freedom Day today.

In 1521, on the island of Mactan in the Philippines, the explorer Ferdinand Magellan was killed in battle with the warriors of the chief Lapulapu. His ships would sail on and complete the first voyage around the world without him.

In 1667, the poet John Milton, blind and poor, sold the rights to Paradise Lost for ten pounds.

In 1749, in London's Green Park, twelve thousand people gathered to hear Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks. The fireworks set a pavilion ablaze, but the music was magnificent.

And in 2005, the Airbus A380, the largest passenger plane ever built, took off for the first time from Toulouse.

Today the Netherlands turns orange for King's Day, with street markets and music everywhere.

events.text: Ferdinand Magellan is killed in the Philippines.
John Milton sells the rights to Paradise Lost for ten pounds.
Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks is first performed in London.

Boxer Rocky Marciano retires undefeated.

Xerox introduces the Star computer with a mouse and windows.

births.text: Mary Wollstonecraft, English writer (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman)
Samuel Morse, American inventor of Morse code
Ulysses S. Grant, 18th President of the United States
Wallace Carothers, American inventor of nylon

facts.text: Nelson Mandela cast his first ever vote in 1994, at the age of 75.

names: World Day for Safety and Health at Work
04-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of April in 1789, in the warm waters of the South Pacific, Fletcher Christian and a band of sailors seized HMS Bounty and set Captain William Bligh adrift in a small open boat with eighteen loyal men. Bligh then sailed that tiny boat more than six thousand kilometres to safety, one of the greatest feats of navigation ever.

In 1923, Wembley Stadium in London opened with the FA Cup final. So many people poured in that a police officer on a white horse had to slowly push the crowd back off the pitch.

In 1947, the Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl and five companions set out from Peru on a raft of balsa logs called Kon-Tiki. A hundred and one days later, they reached Polynesia.

In 1967, the boxer Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted into the army to fight in Vietnam. He lost his title, but kept his principles.

And in 2001, an American businessman named Dennis Tito flew to the International Space Station, the world's first space tourist.

events.text: Sailors mutiny aboard HMS Bounty.
The Covenant of the League of Nations is adopted.
Wembley Stadium opens with the famous "White Horse Final".
A vaccine against yellow fever is announced.
Benito Mussolini is executed by Italian partisans.
Thor Heyerdahl sets out on the Kon-Tiki raft.

Muhammad Ali refuses to be drafted into the U.S. Army.
Charles de Gaulle resigns as President of France.

births.text: James Monroe, 5th President of the United States
Harper Lee, American author (To Kill a Mockingbird)

facts.text: The Kon-Tiki raft drifted about 8,000 kilometres across the Pacific in 101 days.
Captain Bligh sailed an open boat with 18 men about 6,700 kilometres to Timor after the Bounty mutiny.

04-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of April in 1429, a seventeen-year-old peasant girl in armour rode into the besieged city of Orléans, bringing food and fresh hope. Within days, Joan of Arc had broken the siege, and France began to believe it could win.

In 1899, a Belgian racing driver named Camille Jenatzy sat in a bullet-shaped electric car called La Jamais Contente, the Never Satisfied, and became the first person to drive faster than one hundred kilometres an hour.

In 1913, a Swedish-American engineer named Gideon Sundback received a patent for his hookless fastener. We call it the zip.

In 1945, American soldiers liberated the Dachau concentration camp.

In 1968, the musical Hair opened on Broadway, singing of peace, love and the dawning of the Age of Aquarius.

And in 2011, Prince William married Catherine Middleton at Westminster Abbey, as two billion people around the world watched on television.

Today is also International Dance Day. Perhaps you might dance a little.

events.text: Joan of Arc arrives at the besieged city of Orléans.
La Jamais Contente becomes the first car to exceed 100 km/h.
A huge rockslide buries part of the town of Frank, Canada.
Gideon Sundback patents the modern zip.
The Easter Rising rebels surrender in Dublin.
American troops liberate Dachau concentration camp.
India and China sign the Panchsheel agreement on peaceful coexistence.
The musical Hair opens on Broadway.
President Nixon releases edited transcripts of the Watergate tapes.
Riots break out in Los Angeles after the Rodney King verdict.

births.text: William Randolph Hearst, American newspaper owner

facts.text: International Dance Day falls on the birthday of Jean-Georges Noverre, creator of modern ballet.
Japan's Shōwa Day honours the birthday of Emperor Hirohito.

04-30.script:
On the thirtieth of April in 1789, on a balcony in New York, George Washington laid his hand on a Bible and took the oath as the first President of the United States. The crowd below roared, and church bells rang across the city.

In 1803, the United States agreed to buy the vast Louisiana Territory from France, doubling the size of the young nation for about three cents an acre.

In 1897, the physicist J. J. Thomson announced that atoms contain tiny charged particles, far smaller than any atom. He had discovered the electron.

In 1945, in his bunker beneath Berlin, with the Red Army only streets away, Adolf Hitler took his own life. The war in Europe would be over within days.

In 1975, the last Americans left Saigon by helicopter from rooftops, and North Vietnamese tanks rolled through the gates of the presidential palace. The Vietnam War was over.

And in 1993, CERN made the software of the World Wide Web free for anyone to use, for ever. That gift made the web we know today.

events.text: George Washington is inaugurated as the first President of the United States.
The United States agrees to the Louisiana Purchase.
Louisiana becomes the 18th U.S. state.
J. J. Thomson announces the discovery of the electron.

CERN makes the World Wide Web free for everyone.

births.text: Dadasaheb Phalke, father of Indian cinema
Carl XVI Gustaf, King of Sweden

facts.text: Dadasaheb Phalke, born today, made India's first full-length feature film, Raja Harishchandra, in 1913.
